result: Beta bursts in human sensorimotor cortex have consistent temporal, spectral, and spatial characteristics. Bursts lasted on average 238 ms (SD=23 ms), occurred predominantly in the lower beta frequency range (spanning ~3 Hz), were most likely to occur in M1 on the posterior bank of the precentral gyrus, and spanned on average 10% of the ROI's surface area (~6 cm²).
evaluation: Claims C33-C36 and C78-C80 provide converging quantitative evidence from MEG data analysis with consistent measurements across subjects. The temporal (C33, C113), spectral (C34, C79, C114), and spatial (C35, C36, C80, C117, C118) characteristics are well-documented with specific values and standard deviations, supported by Figure 1.

result: Beta burst activity in sensorimotor cortex propagates along two orthogonal axes: one anterior-posterior (a-p) axis traversing the central sulcus perpendicularly (means of 66° and 248°), and one medial-lateral (m-l) axis running parallel to the central sulcus (means of 142° and 324°). These propagation patterns were well described by a mixture of four von Mises functions.
evaluation: Claims C6, C50-C53, C62, and C81 present the core finding about propagation axes with specific quantitative measurements. The von Mises function fitting (C53) provides statistical support, and the orthogonal relationship is consistently reported across claims. Figure 4a provides visual confirmation of the bimodal distribution.

result: 79.6% (SD=2.4%) of bursts showed a dominant planar propagation orientation, and real sensorimotor beta burst activity exhibited significantly stronger planar spatiotemporal structure than spectrally matched surrogate data (all 100 bursts p<0.01).
evaluation: Claims C42 and C43 provide quantitative evidence for planar propagation with specific percentages and statistical significance testing against surrogate data. The surrogate comparison (C43) provides strong evidence that the observed patterns are not artifacts, addressing a key methodological concern.

result: The two propagation axes are characterized by distinct anatomical and physiological features. Bursts propagating medial-laterally have higher amplitude (m-l: M=0.98 vs a-p: M=0.94, p<0.012), larger extent (m-l: M=-0.33 vs a-p: M=-0.53, p<0.012), and slower propagation speeds (m-l: M=2.72 m/s vs a-p: M=2.97 m/s, p<0.017). Bursts propagating along a-p are located predominantly in M1 near the central sulcus, while m-l bursts are centered in S1.
evaluation: Claims C7, C64-C69, and C82 provide comprehensive statistical comparisons between the two propagation axes with specific values, standard deviations, and p-values. The spatial location differences (C67-C69) are supported by principal component analysis with significant Kolmogorov-Smirnov test results (all ps<0.001), as shown in Figure 4c.

result: Pre- and post-movement beta bursts can be distinguished by their characteristics. Post-movement bursts occur more frequently (60.9% vs 34.3%, p=0.012), have larger amplitude (M=0.974 db vs M=0.898 db, p=0.012), larger extent (M=-0.480 vs M=-0.719, p=0.012), and slower propagation speed (M=2.69 m/s vs M=2.90 m/s, p=0.012) compared to pre-movement bursts.
evaluation: Claims C8, C70-C72, C74, C83, and C120-C122, C126 provide consistent quantitative evidence with statistical significance (all p=0.012) for differences between pre- and post-movement bursts. The measurements are specific with means and standard deviations across individuals, supported by Figure 5b.

result: Pre- and post-movement beta bursts have distinct functional roles, as suggested by their different physiological markers. The observed differences in amplitude, extent, and propagation speed indicate that pre- and post-movement bursts may share similar generator processes but exhibit more and stronger bursts post-movement.
evaluation: Claims C9, C84, C131, and C132 make functional inferences from the observed physiological differences. While the physiological differences are well-supported (see previous result), the claim about distinct functional roles (C9, C84) is speculative and not directly tested. C132 is explicitly marked as speculative inference, acknowledging this limitation.

result: Pre- and post-movement bursts propagate along the same propagation axes. The average spatial location and frequency center were not significantly different between pre- and post-movement bursts (all ps>0.1), and propagation directions were not significantly different (U2: M=0.088, range=0.025-0.190; 8/8 ps>0.1). The directions for pre-movement (a-p: 68/246°; m-l: 148/315°) did not differ from post-movement (a-p: 66/248°; m-l: 142/325°).
evaluation: Claims C73, C75, C76, and C128 provide statistical evidence for the absence of differences in propagation direction between pre- and post-movement bursts using Watson's U2 test. The quantitative angles (C76) show minimal differences, and the consistency is noted across all 8 subjects. This finding is consistent with cited animal studies (C75, C128).

result: Validation analyses demonstrate that propagation directions can be estimated with sufficient accuracy from MEG recordings. Under noise-free conditions, propagation direction can be estimated accurately from regular meshes, with mean error roughly twice as large for random meshes. Using the real mesh, there was an average error of 7° between true and estimated propagation direction, with little variability across individuals (SD=0.5°) and angles (SD=1.5°). Error was lower for bursts with larger apparent spatial width.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide comprehensive validation through simulation studies comparing different mesh types and spatial sampling rates. The quantitative error estimates (C47) with low variability and the relationship between burst size and accuracy (C48) demonstrate methodological rigor. Figure 3 provides visual support for these validation analyses.

result: The propagation axes identified are reliable and statistically significant. The length and direction of the von Mises functions were highly reproducible across split-halves (percentage difference in length: M=4.32%, SD=3.86%; angular difference: M=2.2°, SD=2.8°), and the length of the real von Mises functions was significant while correcting for multiple comparisons at p<0.01.
evaluation: Claims C56 and C57 provide statistical evidence for reliability through split-half analysis (500 repetitions) and significance through permutation testing (5000 permutations). The small angular differences (M=2.2°) and percentage differences in length (M=4.32%) demonstrate high reproducibility, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

result: Control analyses suggest that differences in bursts' apparent spatial width are not merely due to differences in SNR across and/or within sessions, but are primarily due to differences in the spatial distribution of cortical activity. While burst amplitude and burst apparent spatial width are positively correlated within sessions (Pearson's r: M=0.749, SD=0.056, all ps<0.001), diverse phase lags across space within bursts are unlikely to arise simply from amplitude scaling of a single source.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41 address a critical methodological concern about whether spatial extent reflects true cortical activity or SNR artifacts. The absence of correlations across sessions (C38) combined with the presence of phase lags (C40) provides converging evidence. However, the positive correlation within sessions (C39) requires the phase lag observation to rule out simple amplitude scaling.

result: Control analyses demonstrate that beamformer weights contribute to, but do not solely explain, the observed propagation directions. Significant correlations (Pearson's r: M=0.61, SD=0.27, all ps<0.05) were found between latency of critical points before and after regressing out main components of spatial variability in LCMV weights. Additionally, potential spatial sampling bias does not bias the propagation analysis.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 address important methodological concerns about beamformer artifacts. The moderate correlation (r=0.61) after regressing out beamformer weight variability (C58) indicates that beamformer weights contribute but don't fully explain the results (C59). The spatial sampling bias control (C60-C61) provides additional methodological validation.

result: The observed propagation axes do not align with the directions showing the smallest or largest error when estimating direction from noise-free gradients on the same surface mesh and spatial burst properties, indicating that mesh properties do not drive the observed propagation direction.
evaluation: Claims C54 and C55 provide evidence that the observed propagation patterns are not artifacts of the mesh geometry. By comparing observed directions with simulation results showing where errors would be minimized/maximized, the authors demonstrate that the biological signal is distinct from methodological artifacts.

result: Propagation speeds are compatible with previous reports and anatomical properties. Propagation speed derived from folded surfaces is roughly twice as fast as from inflated surfaces (consistent with folding factor of 2.2), and the observed speeds (inflated: M=2.61 m/s; folded: M=4.90 m/s) are compatible with previous reports from human and non-human primates and with axonal conduction speeds of myelinated cortical white matter fibers, suggesting an active role for macro-scale travelling burst activity in intra-areal communication.
evaluation: Claims C109-C111 provide quantitative comparisons with previous literature and known anatomical properties. The folding factor comparison (C109) is consistent with prior reports. However, C112's inference about functional role is speculative and goes beyond what the speed measurements alone can support, though it's appropriately framed as a suggestion.

result: There is no evidence that burst characteristics relate to reaction time in these data (all ps>0.1).
evaluation: Claim C77 reports a negative finding with appropriate statistical thresholds. While negative results are less definitive than positive findings, the claim is appropriately stated and the statistical threshold is clearly reported.

result: There were no significant differences between beta bursts around index or middle finger movement.
evaluation: Claim C37 reports a negative finding from post hoc analysis. While the specific statistical test and p-value are not provided, this is presented as a supplementary observation rather than a primary result.

result: The study analyzed 123-611 trials per participant (M=438.5, SD=151.0) in which correct key presses were made with right index or middle finger in response to congruent imperative stimuli and high coherence visual cues. Bursts were identified over a 4 s time window (-2 to 2 s relative to button press) in the beta frequency range (13-30 Hz) using session-specific amplitude thresholding and 5D clustering.
evaluation: Claims C31 and C32 describe the experimental design and data analysis parameters. These are straightforward methodological descriptions that are well-documented in the manuscript and figures.

result: There is no evidence that the difference in propagation speed between pre- and post-movement bursts is mediated through differences in frequency or spatial location of bursts, as both metrics are comparable for pre- and post-movement bursts.
evaluation: Claim C127 rules out potential confounds for the observed speed differences. This is supported by C73 which shows no significant differences in spatial location and frequency center (all ps>0.1). This control analysis strengthens the interpretation of the speed differences.

result: The finding that pre- and post-movement bursts propagate along the same axis provides further evidence that the propagation of burst activity is constrained by the underlying connectivity.
evaluation: Claim C130 is an inference drawn from the consistency of propagation axes across conditions (C128). While this is an interpretation rather than a direct observation, it is a reasonable inference supported by the data and consistent with anatomical knowledge about cortical connectivity.

result: The temporal and spectral properties of beta bursts are broadly in line with previous reports, with variation in absolute values being strongly dependent on how bursts are operationalized. A discrepancy with Little et al., 2019 regarding temporal burst duration is explained by different thresholding approaches (they used different thresholds for pre- and post-movement bursts, while the current study used the same threshold).
evaluation: Claims C115, C123 compare findings with previous literature with appropriate citations. Claims C124-C125 address a specific discrepancy with methodological explanation. The comparison is fair and the methodological explanation (C125) is reasonable, though it's presented as the authors' belief rather than tested directly.

result: The results extend previous invasive recordings by showing that burst activity can travel across sensory and motor cortices and bridge across functionally distinct brain areas. The dominant propagation axes conform to known anatomical networks: an anterior-posterior network comprising dorsal premotor cortex, primary motor cortex, and primary sensory cortex, and a medial-lateral network spanning across medial and lateral dorsal premotor cortex, supplementary motor area cortex, and caudal portions of ventral premotor cortex.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 interpret the findings in the context of known anatomy with appropriate citations. C93 is a reasonable inference about extending previous work given the larger spatial scale of the current study. C94-C95 link observed propagation patterns to established anatomical networks, though this is interpretive rather than directly tested.

result: While approaching the spatial limits of human MEG, the data indicate the possibility of locating beta activity within the sensorimotor cortex.
evaluation: Claim C119 is a cautious inference about the spatial resolution capabilities demonstrated by the study. The acknowledgment of approaching spatial limits shows appropriate awareness of methodological constraints while claiming the demonstrated capability.

result: Control analyses suggest that beamformer weights can affect bursts' spatial width and propagation direction but are not driving the observed effects. The estimated propagation direction correlates significantly with the propagation direction obtained after regressing out main components of spatial variability in beamformer weights.
evaluation: Claims C147, C148, and C151 address methodological concerns about beamformer artifacts through control analyses. The significant correlation after regression (C147) and the conclusion that beamformer weights contribute but don't drive effects (C148, C151) are appropriately cautious interpretations of the control analyses.

result: Beta oscillations in human sensorimotor cortex are hallmark signatures of healthy and pathological movement. In single trials, beta oscillations include bursts of intermittent, transient periods of high-power activity that have been linked to motor, perceptual, sensory function, and pathophysiological movement.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C14 summarize established knowledge in the field with appropriate citations. These are background claims that set the context for the study rather than novel findings. The citations support these well-established observations.

result: The precise spatial, spectral, and temporal structure of beta burst events remains unclear, and their functional role is not well understood. In humans, the precise properties of beta bursts and whether their high-amplitude activity comprise distinct spatiotemporal gradients remain unclear.
evaluation: Claims C4, C15, and C30 identify gaps in current knowledge that motivate the study. These are appropriate statements of what is unknown in the field and provide justification for the research questions addressed.

result: All participants were free of neurological or psychiatric disorders, right-handed, and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Subject-specific head-casts were used to optimize co-registration and reduce head movements, thereby significantly improving SNR. Individual cortical surface meshes were extracted using FreeSurfer from multiparameter maps and were down-sampled by a factor of 10 (vertices: M=30,095, SD=2665; faces: M=60,182, SD=5331) and smoothed (5 mm).
evaluation: Claims C152-C155 describe participant characteristics and methodological procedures. These are straightforward descriptions of the experimental setup and preprocessing steps that are standard practice and well-documented.
